description: We’re equa.ai, a team that enjoys coding and working with data. We want to build a simple web app that uses NASA satellite data and local soil information to help farmers decide what to grow next. Join us if you’d like to work with real NASA data and build a working prototype together. We’re looking for teammates who can help with web development, data analysis, or UI design.
summary:
Field Tracker is a web app for farmers in northern Kazakhstan. It opens without an account and works on a phone screen.

The farmer picks a place on the map or draws their field. The app reads daily NASA POWER data going back to 1981 and shows how this growing season compares with every earlier season at the same spot: the longest dry spell, the number of frost days, and root-zone soil moisture. Each one is marked Normal, Watch or Unusual.

On the Crops tab the farmer enters their current three-year rotation and picks a priority, either improving soil or saving water. The app puts it next to two alternatives, such as adding a legume, and counts in how many of the last 45 years each crop had enough days between frosts. Every option card explains why it was suggested and lists the evidence and its sources (NASA POWER, FAO, Government of Saskatchewan). It also states what the tool does not know and what to ask an agronomist.

The challenge asks for rotations that hold up as frost, heat and dry spells shift. Field Tracker answers that with 45 years of local NASA records.
details:
What it does

Field Tracker is a web app for farmers in northern Kazakhstan. It runs in a phone browser and needs no account.

The farmer starts by choosing a place. There are four saved points near Astana, Kokshetau, Kostanay and Petropavl. The farmer can also outline a field on the map or type its coordinates.

The Season tab shows three cards for the growing season (1 April to 30 September):

  • the longest dry spell,
  • the number of frost days,
  • the average root-zone soil moisture.

Each value is ranked against every season at the same point since 1981. A season among the worst 25% is marked Watch, among the worst 10% Unusual; these cut-offs are our own choice. Each card says where the number comes from and lists a few things the farmer can do, taken from FAO guidance. Any past season can be opened and compared.

On the Crops tab the farmer enters a three-year rotation and picks a priority: improve soil or save water. The app sets that rotation beside up to two alternatives built from simple rules, such as putting a legume where a cereal follows a cereal. Near Kostanay, spring wheat had a long enough frost-free season in 41 of the last 45 years, and field pea in 45 of 45.

Each option shows why it was suggested, the evidence and its source, what the tool does not know, and what to ask an agronomist. A short summary in plain English sits on top, written by Google Gemini from the same numbers. The app throws the summary away if it contains a number that is not on the cards.

Data and how we checked it

All weather and soil values come from the NASA POWER daily API: minimum and maximum air temperature, corrected precipitation and root-zone soil wetness, from 1981 onward. Saved points work offline because their data is stored in the app; a drawn field triggers a live request. NASA GIBS MODIS imagery and NDVI appear on the map as a visual layer only, and no result is calculated from them. Crop growing periods and water needs come from FAO, and legume nitrogen figures from the Government of Saskatchewan.

To see how far reanalysis can be trusted here, we compared POWER at Kostanay with the NOAA GHCN station Kustanai, about 1 km away. Across 25–26 seasons the correlation was 0.80 for rain totals, 0.87 for the longest dry spell and 0.89 for frost days. The main results for the four points were also recomputed separately in Python, and automated tests check the app against them.

Tools

TypeScript, Next.js and React, with Leaflet for the map. Tests run in Vitest, the independent recalculation was written in Python, and the app is hosted on Vercel. The in-app summary uses the Google Gemini API.

AI assistants (Claude) helped write code, check data sources and draft text. The idea and the choice of region came from the team.

What makes it different

Most farm tools show this year’s weather. We compare this season with the same spot’s own 45-year record, so “dry” means dry for that place. The rotation comparison turns the same record into a simple count: in how many past years would this crop have had enough days between frosts?

We also put the gaps on screen. Every card has a section called “What this tool does not know”.

What we weighed

  • Resolution: a POWER grid cell is roughly 50 km across, so the app talks about the area, not a single field.
  • Data source: POWER is a model reanalysis, not station data, which is why we ran the station check.
  • Global reference values: FAO crop values are global guides, and the nitrogen figures come from Canada, so both are labelled.
  • No outcome claims: there is no yield, price or income prediction, because we have no data for it.
  • Offline demo: the saved points had to work without internet.
  • Phone screens: text had to stay readable on a phone screen 375 px wide.

Intended impact

We want a farmer to see in a few minutes how unusual this season was where they farm. Then they can bring two or three sourced rotation options to their agronomist, instead of starting from a blank page.

Our repository
